trajectory.title: Checking
trajectory.description: Computers run 15 real brain maps and give receipts anyone can re-check. This is the living cloud's first working service.

trajectory.title: Listening
trajectory.description: Listener boxes near forests, reefs and farms. Built and tested in the lab. Next step: proving they work outdoors.

trajectory.title: Thinking, done by nature
trajectory.description: Fast, low-power computing done by living things. Other labs already sell computers built from living nerve cells, which shows living things can compute. We would only work with wild nature, never attach anything, and only with proof and permission.

trajectory.title: Remembering in DNA
trajectory.description: One gram of DNA can hold about 215 million gigabytes. Nobody yet knows a gentle way to do this in living nature. Finding one is part of the plan.

anatomy.title: Cells — AI companions
anatomy.description: One for each forest, reef or field. Today it is a simple program that keeps records and follows its guardian's choices. Learning its home's patterns comes later.

anatomy.title: Senses — listener boxes
anatomy.description: They hear birds, bugs and plant clicks, and use AI ears to tell the sounds apart.

anatomy.title: Nerves — agreeing and passing notes
anatomy.description: Boxes check with each other before anything counts, and pass sealed notes along.

anatomy.title: Memory — receipts
anatomy.description: Everything it learns is sealed so anyone can re-check it.

anatomy.title: Brain — brain maps
anatomy.description: Maps of real animal nerves, run on regular computers. No animal is involved.

anatomy.title: Metabolism — credit
anatomy.description: Credit flows back to the nature that shared, like food that keeps a body going.

anatomy.title: Immune system — the brakes
anatomy.description: Rules that block anything harmful or anything nature has not agreed to.

evolve.title: Learn from nature's designs
evolve.description: In real brains, each nerve links to only a few others. Copying that idea made our brain maps 46 to 5,900 times smaller than the usual way, and they use about 70 times less energy on big maps.

evolve.title: Tune itself
evolve.description: Boxes already sleep most of the day and wake for the dawn and dusk choruses. Next, the organism learns on its own when to listen and what to keep.

evolve.title: Prove every step
evolve.description: A new version can only take over if its receipts prove it uses less power, space or time. Our energy test already works. It gives the same result every time it runs.

evolve.title: Move work to nature
evolve.description: Step by step, jobs can move from computer chips to living systems — only with proof and permission. Nothing is attached and nothing is forced.

thesis: Nature already beats computers at using little energy and packing data tightly. The big question is whether it can win at speed and size too. Every step we take comes with a receipt.

axes.today: simulation on silicon; organism compute is not allowed
axes.field: biological synapse ~1–100 pJ/event vs TrueNorth ~26 pJ (Science 2014) and Loihi ~23.6 pJ (IEEE Micro 2018); per watt, a brain does ~10–10,000× more operations than the fastest supercomputer

axes.today: one step at a time, silicon wins — our API answers in milliseconds, on the record
axes.field: wetware already reads and writes living neurons in under a millisecond (Cortical Labs CL1, vendor-reported — ABC 2025 · Forbes 2025); in-place listening has no upload delay, because the sensor sits where the signal is; brains finish complex perception in ~100 ms through parallelism, not clock speed

axes.today: serial FLOPs: worse — measured, on the record
axes.field: a brain handles an estimated 10¹³–10¹⁶ operations/s on ~20 W (Sandberg 2016 · PNAS 2021); El Capitan does 1.8×10¹⁸ FLOP/s on 29.7 MW (TOP500) — that is ~10×–10,000× more operations per watt for the brain. Synaptic events are not FLOPs, and turning them into useful work is the open problem

axes.today: the evidence ledger — receipts, not bulk data
axes.field: DNA reaches 215 PB/g (Erlich, Science 2017) vs conventional media; reading it back already got 3,200× faster (Bar-Lev, Nature Machine Intelligence 2025); the non-invasive read/write interface is unknown — and enters only with consent
